distinguishing_feature: Amebic cystitis is caused by Entamoeba histolytica, usually in a traveller or endemic-area resident; acute cystitis is bacterial (E. coli, Klebsiella) with no amebic exposure history.
Diphtheritic cystitis is caused by Corynebacterium diphtheriae and forms a pseudomembrane on the bladder mucosa; acute cystitis is a common bacterial UTI without pseudomembrane formation.

Chlamydial infection is an STI (Chlamydia trachomatis), often with urethral discharge and sexual exposure history; acute cystitis is non-sexually-transmitted bacterial infection, confirmed by standard urine culture.

Trichomonal infection is caused by Trichomonas vaginalis (often with frothy vaginal discharge); chlamydial infection is caused by Chlamydia trachomatis (often with mucopurulent discharge) — differentiated by STI swab.
Candidal infection is fungal (Candida species), usually in an immunocompromised or antibiotic-exposed patient; acute bacterial cystitis is bacterial, confirmed by urine culture with bacterial growth.
Irradiation cystitis follows a history of pelvic radiotherapy; acute cystitis has no radiation exposure history and responds to antibiotics, which irradiation cystitis does not.
Presence of visible haematuria on urinalysis is the sole distinguishing feature — same acute bacterial cystitis, different degree of mucosal involvement.
Presence of haematuria on urinalysis distinguishes these — same chronic interstitial cystitis, IC with hematuria has mucosal bleeding seen on cystoscopy (Hunner lesions more likely).
Interstitial cystitis is chronic (>6 weeks), culture-negative, and does not respond to antibiotics; acute cystitis is short-duration, culture-positive, and antibiotic-responsive.

Interstitial cystitis affects the whole bladder wall with Hunner lesions on cystoscopy; trigonitis is localised inflammation of the bladder trigone only, seen as epithelial changes at the trigone on cystoscopy.

Overactive bladder is a urological syndrome with urinary urgency/frequency driven by detrusor overactivity; hypertensive urgency is a cardiovascular emergency driven by severely elevated blood pressure — the word 'urgency' is unrelated.

Overactive bladder has urgency with frequency but no bladder pain; interstitial cystitis has chronic bladder/pelvic pain as the dominant symptom with urgency secondary to pain rather than detrusor overactivity.

Central diabetes insipidus is caused by insufficient ADH secretion from the hypothalamus/pituitary and responds to desmopressin; nephrogenic DI is caused by renal resistance to ADH and does NOT respond to desmopressin — the water deprivation test distinguishes them.
Both are renal failure complicating spontaneous abortion; incomplete abortion has retained products of conception confirmed on ultrasound, complete abortion has no retained products.

Induced termination is a completed elective procedure; failed attempted termination is an elective procedure that failed to terminate the pregnancy — context from the clinical record distinguishes them.
Ectopic/molar pregnancy has a tubal or trophoblastic origin confirmed on ultrasound/hCG pattern; incomplete spontaneous abortion involves intrauterine retained products.
Both are hypertensive CKD at stage 5/ESRD; the 'with heart failure' variant has concurrent clinical heart failure (dyspnoea, reduced EF on echo) in addition to the renal disease.
Congenital renal failure is present from birth (neonatal/infant presentation, congenital anomalies of kidney); hypertensive CKD develops progressively in adults with chronic hypertension.
Initial encounter is the first active treatment visit after trauma; subsequent encounter is any follow-up visit for the same injury event.
Subsequent encounter is during active treatment of the original injury; sequela is a late effect persisting or arising after the acute injury has been treated and the healing period is complete.
Presence of haematuria on urinalysis is the only distinguishing feature — same inflammation of the bladder trigone, different degree of mucosal bleeding.
Trigonitis is localised to the trigone (confirmed on cystoscopy); acute cystitis involves diffuse bladder mucosal inflammation with positive urine culture.
Same radiation-induced bladder injury; haematuria is present in the 'with haematuria' variant, indicating more severe mucosal damage or telangiectasia formation.
Irradiation cystitis has a clear history of pelvic radiotherapy; other cystitis with haematuria has no radiation history and may represent chemical, viral, or idiopathic causes.
Presence of haematuria distinguishes these two — same non-specific cystitis of unspecified cause.

Other cystitis is a short-term or unspecified condition without confirmed interstitial pathology; interstitial cystitis is a chronic (>6 week) diagnosis of exclusion with characteristic cystoscopy findings.
Defined purely by gestational timing: first trimester is <13 weeks, second trimester is 13–26 weeks — same clinical entity, different gestational stage.
Third trimester is during the antenatal period (>26 weeks, pre-delivery); complicating childbirth is diagnosed during the active labour and delivery event.
Complicating childbirth is during active delivery; complicating the puerperium is the postnatal period (up to 6 weeks after delivery) — same gestational proteinuria, different timing.
Unspecified trimester is used when the gestational age at diagnosis is not documented; first trimester is used when gestational age is confirmed as <13 weeks.
Isolated proteinuria with glomerular abnormality is a non-pregnancy glomerular disease; gestational proteinuria is specifically pregnancy-related and resolves postpartum.

Primary membranous nephropathy has characteristic sub-epithelial immune deposits on renal biopsy (PLA2R antibody positive); isolated proteinuria with minor glomerular abnormality has minimal biopsy changes without membranous pattern.
Postural incontinence leaks specifically on change of body position; other specified incontinence covers mixed or atypical patterns that do not fit standard stress/urge/postural categories.

Postural incontinence is the primary urological leakage disorder; irritant dermatitis is a secondary skin complication from prolonged urine contact — both can coexist but the dermatitis is not the urinary diagnosis.
Other specified incontinence is the underlying leakage disorder; irritant dermatitis is the downstream skin consequence of ongoing leakage.

BPH with LUTS has documented lower urinary tract symptoms (poor stream, frequency, nocturia, hesitancy); BPH without LUTS is an incidental finding on exam/imaging with no symptomatic urinary complaints yet.
BPH occurs in males with prostate enlargement on DRE/ultrasound; urethral stricture (female) is a narrowing of the female urethra, confirmed on urethrogram or cystoscopy — different anatomy and sex.

Post-traumatic bulbous urethral stricture involves the bulbar urethra (commonest site for straddle injury); membranous urethral stricture involves the membranous urethra (typically from pelvic fracture injury to the posterior urethra).
Membranous stricture is in the posterior urethra (pelvic fracture mechanism); anterior urethral stricture covers both bulbar and penile urethra strictures from straddle or instrumentation injury.
Postprocedural stricture follows a documented urological procedure (catheterisation, surgery); other urethral stricture (female) has no identified postprocedural cause.
Other urethral stricture (female) has an identifiable but non-postprocedural/non-traumatic cause; unspecified has no documented aetiology.
Post-void dribbling occurs specifically after micturition ends due to residual urine in the bulbar urethra; BPH with LUTS causes poor stream and hesitancy throughout voiding, not just at the end.

Post-void dribbling is a functional pooling of urine in the bulbar urethra without a fixed structural narrowing; post-traumatic bulbous stricture is a fixed narrowing confirmed on urethrogram — both can coexist after perineal trauma.
